speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I direct my question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The director general of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in Saskatchewan has said that the department has been illegally taking children away from their parents in Saskatchewan. There are some 700 children in the care of the department in Saskatchewan, and the parents of these children, in all likelihood, never had the right to a hearing regarding the apprehension of their children. We take them on a humanitarian basis and place them in foster homes or institutions, about 60 per cent of which are Indian homes or institutions.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada. subsubtopic: IMPORTATION AND DISTRIBUTION OF PORNOGRAPHIC MATERIAL-GOVERNMENT ACTION

They will have an announcement to make in a short while with regard, I think, to a very useful arrangement they have entered into with some of the distributors. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I remarked a few moments ago, 1 have often stated that my well known preference is to arrange for the planning of the House by agreement. However, I have had more than one occasion in the past to observe that there are, indeed, times, either for reasons of ideology or just plain politics, when one or more group in this House may find it of advantage to fail to so participate in the affairs of the House so that the House cannot come to an agreement or decision on measures before it. It is for the purpose of dealing with just this kind of intransigence that we have this particular procedure and that this motion is made.
It is particularly regrettable in this instance that an agreement was not possible. The amendments to the Income Tax Act incorporated in Bill C-22 are numerous. They are important in their over-all impact on Canada, and important to the
Income Tax
many thousands of Canadians they affect directly. These taxpayers are now telling us to get on with our business so that they can get on with theirs. I believe the opposition expressed in some corners of the House to particular measures proposed in this legislation has been ill-advised. It has impaired the orderly and effective conduct of the business of parliament and it is not serving the interests of the country.
It has been claimed that the bill, particularly with its changes which raise the level of deductible contributions to pension plans, benefits only the well-to-do. The facts do not support this claim. In 1975, average family income in this country was $16,263. In 1976, of course, this figure would have been higher. Yet the simple arithmetic of the new maximum contributions to registered pension plans and registered retirement savings plans tells us that they will benefit taxpayers with incomes above $12,500. Several hundred thousand middle income taxpayers in this country, taxpayers whose incomes are average by this modest measurement, are helped by these changes. Far from a gift to the privileged, the increases simply restore the real value of limits set for contributions when tax reform was introduced five years ago.
They do no more than make up for the erosion brought about by inflation. Furthermore, many pension contracts require percentage contributions by employees which now exceed the old limits under the Income Tax Act. Without the changes proposed in this bill, these employees will be making contributions to their retirement which are disallowed as deductions, in other words, contributions which will have to be made out of after-tax income.
The bill also provides for a doubling of deductible child care expenses. In this regard I wish to refer to a report which appeared in the Globe and Mail of Saturday last in which it was alleged by a group in Ottawa that there was discrimination as between men and women in the application of these particular measures by favouring a single father to the extent of $1,560 per year for each child, as opposed to a $1,000 maximum for a woman. I would point out that that report is entirely erroneous; the application of the law is the same in both cases.
Almost all of the quarter of a million Canadians who claim the child care allowance stand to benefit from the increase in annual limits to $1,000 per child and $4,000 per family. None of the tax returns taking advantage of these increases can be processed by Revenue Canada until this legislation is approved. The measures in this bill are based on a budget introduced fully eight months ago. It has had the benefit of detailed examination in the House and in the country. All we accomplish by further delay is to prolong uncertainty for taxpayers and delay the decisions that thousands of individuals would like to make with respect to their planning of investments and their planning for retirement.
2544

January 31, 1977
Income Tax
There are other changes in this legislation which will improve our tax system. The bill helps the small businessmen of this country, increasing the annual business income, subject to the low rate of corporate tax, to $150,000 from $100,000, and increasing cumulative income eligible for the low rate to $750,000 from $500,000. The bill introduces a new and fairer tax regime for charities. The changes will ensure, as far as possible, that tax exempt amounts flowing to charities are used as efficiently as possible and for strictly charitable purposes.
The bill provides for a simpler tax calculation affecting five million Canadians, many of them elderly people on limited retirement incomes who are able to make use of the interest and dividend reduction, pension and disability deductions and the special exemption for those over 65. The bill imposes a 10 per cent surtax for 1976 on individuals whose taxes exceed $8,000, a provision clearly based on ability to pay, affecting all taxpayers with incomes above $30,000. There was an erroneous report, attributed to the Canadian Press over the weekend, that this bill repeats the surtax. The very opposite is true. Unless this bill is passed, the surtax, which some hon. members say they favour, will not be imposed at all.
Hear, hear!

In fact, the bill imposes the surtax as a supportive measure to the decisions made pursuant to the anti-inflation program introduced somewhat over a year ago.
I have mentioned only the most obvious reasons why the bill needs the approval of parliament. We are approaching the February 28 deadline when taxpayers must make their decisions on retirement plans and finalize their arrangements with trustees. Increasing numbers of other taxpayers are in position to complete their tax returns and to claim refunds, but hesitate to do so because they are affected by other measures in the bill. More than the usual degree of uncertainty already faces individuals and corporations in the conduct of their affairs at this time. Surely it is our responsibility as members of the House to deal as soon as possible with this legislation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) indicated that the planning of the business of the House should be by way of agreement. Fortunately, that has characterized most of the arrangements for the business of the House, I think, and I know from the reputation, reasonableness, approachability and flexibility that it is much out of character for this man to be playing the Madame Defarge of parliament in moving this motion.
I was a little disturbed that, when he talked in the course of his remarks and used the phrase "in some quarters of the House" with respect to Bill C-22, he did not identify the quarters of the House from which an attitude of intransigence emanates, as he said; because I think it is fair to say-and I think there will be agreement even from those on the government side-that with respect to Bill C-22 the official opposi-

tion, the Progressive Conservative party, has not dealt in a way that could be styled intransigent, by any stretch of the meaning of that word, because there is recognition that although the bill is long and complex, it is important to Canadians.
I would not want to rise in my place and say that there will never be a period in the life of parliament when the use of the guillotine would not be necessary. There are occasions when the use of the guillotine is perhaps necessary, and it is up to the government of the day to make up its mind, when it finds it is necessary, and to suffer the consequences of its actions on that decision.
But the question that has to be asked by this parliament every time a motion of this nature is put is whether a case has been made out by the government for invoking what is unusual under our rules and traditions, in terms of our parliamentary history. The fact of the matter is that this guillotine motion, under our rules and traditions, has not been used very often. If the government has a problem with respect to this situation, it is not as a result of any intransigence, I respectfully suggest, on the part of the opposition but, perhaps, because of the way this session began. This is the first session, in the memory of parliamentarians who have been here longer than I have, in which parliament did not receive at the beginning of the session, in the throne speech, a list of the priorities or important legislation of the government.
As a result, we started on the wrong foot. There was no evidence whatsoever of any planning of the session by the government, nor any indication of what was considered important. This was distressing to us who, having returned to parliament at a time when the economic problems of this country were not getting any better but were, in fact, getting much worse, were faced by a government which gave no evidence whatsoever that during a long parliamentary recess they had even considered them.
As I have described before, there was no evidence of any action on legislation dealing with such problems as unemployment, inflation or lack of productivity. In fact, the situation could only be described as a legislative wasteland. If you go day by day through the debates during the fall of this session of parliament, you will see that we jumped from bill to bill- one day on this bill, one day on another. There was complete lack of any sense of direction in the mind of the government, which was translated into lack of leadership in terms of the business of the House. It is a fact that only on January 24, when we returned from the Christmas recess, we received any indication that there might be some direction to the government's business-almost three months after this session had begun. That is the basis of the problem of the operation of this parliament in this session, and that is the problem with which we are faced.
The Minister of Finance did not mention Bill C-19, the debate on which occupied a total of 15 Vi parliamentary days, almost the whole of the government's legislative period during November. I am referring to the restraints bill. How this occurred, escapes me. That bill had a predecessor in the first session of parliament. We made it clear to the government that

if they withdrew the section dealing with the amendment to the Railway Act, it would pass quickly. We made it clear to them in- the course of the debate and in the course of private discussions that if they removed that section from the bill we would pass it quickly. As a matter of fact, when they finally removed it almost at the end of that period of debate, the bill was passed quickly, but we wasted a tremendous number of parliamentary days.
1 think that is the prime example of stubborness. I do not think it lies at the feet of the government House leader. I think he was dealing with a very stubborn Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) who was finally convinced that while his nannies may get a free ride on government aircraft, this bill was not going to get a free ride in the House. When he was finally prevailed upon to withdraw that section, we withdrew opposition to the bill.
Let me deal, in the few minutes I have left, with Bill C-22, the income tax bill. We are not denying the importance of this piece of legislation, but in point of fact it was left to the tail end of the first part of the second session of this parliament to be dealt with. This important piece of legislation, which affects so many Canadians and respecting which failure to pass would wreak great havoc on economic planning, was first called on November 19. Then it was neglected. The bill was not called again until December 2, and then it was called for debate on three parliamentary days.
If this bill was so important, why did the government order its priority in the way it did? As a matter of fact, up to and including the committee of the whole stage, where the bill now stands, we have only occupied a total of 4'/2 parliamentary days on a very important tax bill. The question which faces us is whether, under these circumstances, we ought in the parliamentary sense to agree to the closing off, or the guillotining, of the debate. The public is guaranteed the results of this bill by motions like this one and perhaps subsequent ones which are going to be brought as the debate proceeds. The public is guaranteed the benefit of the bill in any event, so our question is whether in terms of the traditions of this House, the official opposition ought to agree to this kind of thing.
Having regard to the arrangement of priorities and the lack of leadership in terms of the business of this House, I respectfully submit that this opposition ought not to be the handmaiden to this government's stupidity.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Therefore, we are not prepared to support this closure motion. That is not to say that this would be the case on other occasions, but it is important that we understand that the government has certain responsibilities with respect to the ordering of the business of this House, and those responsibilities, unfortunately-I use the word "unfortunately" because I look upon the government House leader as an adversary only in the professional sense, and certainly not in the personal sense-have not been carried
Income Tax
out. It is unfortunate that that has occurred, and it is also unfortunate that the government has decided to guillotine this piece of legislation after only 41/2 days, using necessity as an excuse which the government must have foreseen some time ago because, after all, the government is the drafter of the bill and, more than that, is the orderer or the business of the House of Commons.
In terms of the role of the opposition, I have always held the view that the opposition has no right whatsoever-no parliamentary right, in any event-to carry on, willy-nilly, prolonging debate on important issues when there is no disagreement in principle. However, when there is disagreement in principle it is the duty of the opposition to carry on the debate and to expose the government, and I think we have carried through on this principle.
Order, please. The hon. member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to make the observation that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) did not spend even 30 seconds attempting to justify this unusual procedure of cutting off debate. I can understand his not spending even 30 seconds, because he knows he has no case whatsoever.
As the House leader for the Conservative party has just said, the reason the government is doing this is that its sense of priorities has been totally wrong, not only with regard to this bill but also with regard to other important national questions. The government brought this bill in for its first serious debate just before the Christmas recess. That is when the debate really began. The Conservative House leader just said we have spent only 4'/2 days on it. This is a bill that the government says is very important. If it is so important, why did we wait since last May, the time of the budget, until just before Christmas for a serious debate? I suggest that the government hoped to slip it through before the Christmas recess.
We do not support the guillotine motion in this case. As has just been indicated, there are times when the government must have a right to act and to exercise its judgment when the opposition is unnecessarily holding up things. In principle we go along with that. Sometimes the government has to act and be responsible for its decisions. However, in this particular instance we say this action is totally unjustified.
We have come back after a month's recess. In that time Canadians talked about all kinds of serious problems, notably the problem of unemployment. But what were the first two steps taken by the government: a debate on televising proceedings in the House, followed by a debate on metrication in certain aspects of agriculture. Those were the priorities of the government. Now the government brings in closure with respect to this financial bill.
The Minister of Finance spent all his time dealing with the substance of the bill and making the best he could of a terrible case for a terrible piece of legislation. In indicating why we oppose the closure motion and why we oppose this bill, I want to talk about four principal clauses in the bill to which we

object. We object to them because they are fundamentally unfair to the people of Canada. I want to deal with the changes in the pension plan, and in particular RRSPs; I want to talk about the child care provisions of the Income Tax Act; the elimination of the special surtax on upper income Canadians, and the effects of indexing.
In talking about these four clauses I want to point out that the information I am going to provide pertains to taxpayers at 1977 levels of taxation on the assumption that those taxpayers will have the average amount of optional deductions for which they may be eligible, and these taxpayers will have two children under the age of sixteen. What are the provisions in this bill? They are being proposed in a country which has growing inequality, in which the poor people have a lower percentage of the total income now than they had 20 years ago, and in which the top segment has a greater percentage of the national income than it had 20 years ago.
Surely that is a disgrace for any government that likes to describe itself as progressive. What are the effects of the changes in the registered pension plan and RRSPs, and how do they affect a $10,000 per year family? That family gets an average saving of $200. A $20,000 a year family saves $500. A taxpayer earning $50,000 per year will save $780. That poor friend of the Liberal party who earns $100,000 will save $940. The benefits in those four categories are in exactly inverse proportions to what they should be in a society which is concerned about economic justice.
What about the child care provisions? Instead of making a direct grant to all people who need child care facilities-and surely they are needed in this country-and by dealing with the need to finance child care in this way, we get profound inequality in terms of effects. What are the benefits in that category for a taxpayer earning $10,000, with two children? He or she will save $200. The $20,000 per year taxpayer will save $250. The $50,000 per year taxpayer will save $390. Then, again, that special friend of the Liberal party, the person earning $100,000 per year, will save $470. That is exactly in inverse proportions to what anyone concerned about compassion and justice would provide.
Then there is the surtax provision that the Minister of Finance touchingly raised a few minutes ago. He correctly pointed out that the surtax will be removed in 1977 on incomes of $30,000 a year or more. I would have thought that instead of drawing attention to that fact, he would have apologized for it. Wage controls will remain on the ordinary workers of the country during that period, but the family with an income of $30,000 a year or more that is supposed to share the burden of the anti-inflation program-and that was the justification given for it when it was introduced a year ago last Christmas-will have the surtax removed. Wage controls will remain for the ordinary people, and I think particularly the non-unionized workers of Canada, while the special surtax for the rich will be removed.

Mr. Speaker, let me show what that little bit of Liberal justice will do. The taxpayer at the $50,000 level will save $420 next year. No one below the $30,000 level will save a cent as a result of this change. The taxpayer at the $80,000 level will save $1,654, and the taxpayer at the $100,000 a year level will save $2,491. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the special surtax which the rich were paying under the controls has been lifted, but wage controls remain. The Minister of Finance said this is peanuts.
That is what you said last year.
Mr. Speaker, $2,491 saved on an income of $100,000 may be peanuts, but to the poor of Canada it is not peanuts.
You have turned yourself completely around. Be honest, now.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has had his chance. Under the provision for indexation carried forward in this act, again the benefits accrue to the people in the various categories I have mentioned. A poor person earning $10,000 a year-and for most parts of Canada that means living below the official poverty level-will save $98; a person earning $20,000 will save $164; the $50,000 a year person will save $450, while the taxpayer with a $100,000 income will save $1,055.
I have gone quickly through the four principal categories of tax benefit provided by this legislation. In each and every one of these categories I have shown that upper income Canadians benefit more than the average or poor Canadian. I say the net effect will be to increase inequality in Canada, instead of reducing it. For that reason, we not only oppose the invocation of the guillotine on this bill, but the bill itself.

Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of
Finance): Mr. Speaker, as members we have a number of jobs to do in this House. We are here to challenge the administration of the government and question ministers as to how they carry out their duties. This House is a sounding-board in which we, as members, can express the concerns of the country and the concerns of our regions and constituents. To a certain point, this chamber is a debating society in which new ideas are put forward. We challenge them, improve them and, speaking for the people of Canada, say what we think ought to be done or what we seek to achieve. But we should not forget-and sometimes we do-that this is a legislative body as well. We have to pass laws. We have the responsibility not only of talking about changes, of talking about what we want to do, but of enacting those changes and incorporating them into laws which will move this country in the direction on which this House decides.
Speaking as a member of a party which is committed to change, which wants to get things done, it is particularly important to me to see this House passing legislation, to see us moving forward and adopting ideas. But we can do this only if we pass laws which will be carried out in the country. We cannot bring about changes just by talking about them. We must bring them about by passing laws. We bring forward laws, vote on them and, hopefully, pass them. During the present session we are talking about human rights legislation, we are talking about improvements in the immigration laws, and about all kinds of economic matters which need to be solved with legislation. We must move ahead; we cannot allow the House to become bogged down with just talk about legislation which will not be dealt with. In other words, the House must face its responsibilities.
The Social Credit party spokesman suggested that the process of time allocation threatens democracy. I put it the other way around: I say that democracy is preserved with time allocation; it is preserved when we bring the House face to face

with its responsibilities and ask it to vote on legislation before it.
People all over this country are calling for a new budget. The economy is not growing as quickly as we want. The world is changing. Our trading partners are implementing new policies which will affect us. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has said that he is working on a new budget. The minister has only had since last May!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This budget provides considerable tax relief across the board. The Social Credit spokesman mentioned, I believe, that the minister had indicated that average income in this country was $16,000 a year. That was not average individual income, but average family income that the minister was referring to, and he said so. And when we are dealing with family incomes of this size, you will note that a considerable number of the important measures in the budget benefit average families.
Mr. Speaker, I think something like five million Canadians, in a normal year, get income tax refunds. That is an approximate number, but not one of these refunds can be paid based on the budget until the bill before us is passed. The Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) cannot issue the order for the refunds to be sent to Canadians unless she has the authority of the legislation which allows such refunds to be made. That legislation must be passed by this House. It is, therefore, urgent that we bring debate on this legislation to an end and to a vote, after which we can move forward and deal with a new budget and all the other important matters which hon. members of the House seek to change through legislation.
Opposition leaders have indicated that sometimes they might approve time allocation, but they have indicated that in this case they cannot approve it. They have taken that position, they say, because the government has not shown enough leadership in moving ahead with existing legislation. Mr. Speaker, in these circumstances how can you exercise leadership without using time allocation? Surely it should not take long to pass a bill of the kind we are discussing. However, it soon became clear that the opposition intended to dig its heels in, prolong debate as long as possible and force the government to do what it has done today; that is, bring in time allocation. As far as I am concerned, time allocation should be used far more often and on a regular basis.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Most Canadians would be astonished to learn that there is no regular method for observing a legislative timetable for bills such as the one before us. There is no other way by which members and the country can know in advance how long legislation will be reviewed, how long it ought to be considered, and when it will ultimately be voted on. I very

much look forward to the day when time allocation will be a regular feature of the rules of procedure and processes of this House.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always interested to hear the comments of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Kaplan). He suggested for example, that the House of Commons is somehow involved in the governmental process. That is the kind of facile argument government spokesmen raise when they argue in favour of restricted debate in the House of Commons. Let us look at this question in its correct perspective. We are debating a motion which will deny the representatives of the people of Canada the opportunity to debate fully, and without restriction, certain measures brought forward by the government. As for the process of governing, it is the responsibility of the government to conduct its day to day activities and involve itself in the consideration of those who question its method of operation.
We are debating our ability to conduct a free and full debate on measures which the government has brought before parliament. These are measures which the government House leader, in his wisdom, has seen fit to bring before parliament. I see the present occasion as an attempt on the part of the government House leader to apply time allocation to all legislation at all stages.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I understand the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) has said on television that he would consider implementing time allocation in various debates. Although the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) is responsible for moving the present motion, the motion itself clearly shows the government's policy. Present circumstances have arisen because of the government's failure during the present and past sessions of parliament to show leadership in this House.
Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to document the legislation which was passed recently. We in the opposition have dealt reasonably with quite a number of items of legislation put forward by the government. The problem is not that the opposition has held up legislation, but that the government has had little of consequence to bring forward. It brought forward certain items it wanted passed, but left in abeyance certain tax matters from the previous session of the present parliament. Last fall it brought forward Bill C-19 which was debated at length. It was delayed until the government acceded to the opposition's request to remove an objectionable clause. After that the House made good progress. Once the government listened to the reasonable arguments of members on my side of the House, Bill C-19 which related to government expenditures soon passed all stages.
We are now dealing with the Income Tax Act. We have spent 4Vi days on it. Second reading is passed and we are now in committee of the whole. We have dealt with the borrowers

and depositors bill, C-16, which took Vh days. We have dealt with the James Bay agreement bill, an important piece of legislation which took Vh days. It has been given second reading.

When we consider that 35 days were spent on government business before Christmas-a total of 40 days up to now-we wonder what strategy the government is following. Why is it bringing down a bill under Standing Order 75 to close debate before even putting Bill C-22 before the House for discussion to determine what progress can be made? Good.

speechtext:
If they feel they have a case, let them speak, and suffer the consequences. The point I am making is that if the government persists in its present approach toward legislation, it will cause itself even more damage than it has already suffered by reason of its bungling and ineptness. By its present course it is showing

little respect for the House of Commons, composed as it is of members who represent all parts of the country.

Mr. Speaker, it is the first time for me to take part in a debate in the House as Minister of National Revenue and member of the cabinet. I think the circumstances of this parliamentary debate fully reflect the worst that can happen to the parliamentary institution when it over emphasizes the significance of procedure instead of keeping in mind the purpose of its very existence-the welfare of Canadians.
I think the wizards of procedure have been particularly well represented this afternoon by the speech of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) who has told us that most Canadians agree on the propositions of Bill C-22 to alleviate the fiscal burden of the taxpayers, but that the parliamentary institution, which means himself and the opposition, had a part to play. The hon. member tried to explain what this part was, even when the Canadian people want this bill passed, and the only thing we have learned from him is how a democratic institution suddenly becomes a lofty sanctuary above the common people.
Or again the list which has just been read by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) is the exact extension of this mentality of the opposition, which, short of ideas, is desperately clinging to procedure. He has given us a reading of the parliamentary works which have been completed since the beginning of this session, taking care to specify that the House took half a day, a day or a day and a half, according to the matter, without telling us at any moment why the opposition wanted to filibuster this bill.
The point of view I want to present this afternoon is that of the least popular of ministers during the first months of the year, the minister responsible for taxation, but I shall do it in a positive manner, because I know that the measures contained in Bill C-22 are beneficial to the majority of Canadians, and not only to a minority. My first concern and my duty as minister is to give Canadian taxpayers the service they are entitled to. That is my first responsibility, and I am not using

the word service just for the pleasure of it, but I am talking about quality, fastness and as few mistakes as possible when our 15,000 civil servants review the many tax returns which have already started to file in for the 1976 taxation year.
It is very important that the House discuss and vote on Bill C-22. A lot of uncertainty and confusion now exists among individuals and families who are about to fill their tax returns. We receive an increasing number of phone calls. People read the papers, watch television, listen to the radio and see that the forms they have already received, earlier than usual this year, that is at the beginning of December, the tax return forms take into consideration, more exactly take for granted that Parliament will adopt Bill C-22, but they know on the other hand that it has not. As minister, I had to proceed with the printing of the amended tax return forms, which take into consideration the provisions of the bill and therefore anticipate the decision of the House, but it is understood that we shall have to amend the forms and to correct the returns filed in by taxpayers if the House does not pass or amend Bill C-22.
As long as Bill C-22 remains undecided, income tax rebates to taxpayers will have to be delayed. As of today, which is the very commencement of the period when returns are received by my department, I have to inform the members of the House that 41 such reports have been put aside because they included one or several of the provisions subject to the amendments included in Bill C-22. This is very unfair, to start with. We hope we will be able to process these returns and we hope to give them priority as soon as the bill is passed. I do not think that the official opposition or any opposition in this chamber wants to penalize taxpayers for our lethargic procedures or lack of ideas.
The major changes of benefit to taxpayers which are being delayed include three points, among others, on which I should like to touch briefly. First is the increase of pension plan contributions, both registered pension plans and registered retirement savings plans. I will not quote misleading statistics in the way the leader of the New Democratic Party did earlier on and confuse Canadians even more. I do know for a fact- and this was clearly illustrated by the information given in December in the course of the debate and earlier this afternoon by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald)-that this favours-

But, of course, nothing will ever be perfect for the NDP. The third and last point-

Let me put forward to the government this very simple thought. When the whole country was worried about the fact that we had been in a recession for over two years, with nothing being done to attack the basic causes of inflation or unemployment, the government presented us when we first came back after the recess with a motion to bring radio and television into the House. No one is opposed to that, but surely there are more serious matters to discuss.
Ask Walter Baker.

The next item on the agenda was metric conversion. Let me remind the House that Canada signed a treaty in 1907, 70 years ago, stating that we were going to bring in metric conversion some day. In 1971, the government passed an order in council saying we were going to put this promise into effect. It only took 70 years to get to that position!
In the last day or so before the recess at Christmas they sneaked in the metric conversion bill which affects the culture, lifestyle and pocketbooks of all farmers in western Canada. They did not think to give a chance in this important legislation to the ordinary, individual workingman in the factories and offices, the small businessman or the farmer, to get a few more bucks of his own to look after his future because these universal plans which we have are not meeting the need. This is good legislation the minister is trying to get through. I do

not quarrel with that. All I ask is, why did they not bring it in on the first day of this session?
Parliament is important. I felt deeply ashamed when I heard members on the government side applauding the fact that what this government needs is closure, closure all the time. They call it allocation of time. You do not drive Canadians to do anything: you lead Canadians. If you want to go back to where the mistake was made, go back to 1968 where the biggest nitwits of all parties got together and brought in the rule changes. That is where you go back to if you want to criticize changes in the rules.
If you want this House to get its business through, allow hon. members to speak on behalf of their people and express their own views. Two years ago, the Manitoba legislature got rid of all this nonsense of trying to restrict elected representatives of the people. There you have a government agreeing with an opposition that the government has a right to govern and the opposition a duty to oppose. Once the government gave to the opposition complete freedom to oppose, the talking slowed down. How they got it was not by allocation of time. They simply sit there all night until the guys are finished talking. Once you get past midnight, the speeches get shorter.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would you approve of that? Would you support that change?

If you want changes in the rules, there is a committee sitting now with all the opportunity of bringing in this type of thing. We are not unreasonable people. If you want to take the estimates and give us back the power to control the spending of money, which parliament is here for, you will be surprised how quickly hon. members can get their difficulties off their minds. However, as long as you take away from parliament the right to speak and the right to vote jon money supply, you cannot expect anything else. Parliament, however, can do its level best to vote against those restrictions and controls.
I think I have said enough, Mr. Speaker. I, personally, do not think the technique of closure is acceptable to a modern-day parliament. I believe that a positive alternative should be adopted; that the leaders and the spokesmen of our parties who deal with these rules should accept the fact they made a big, fat mistake back in 1968, and give in. I said "all parties" because we have nitwits in our party as well as other parties. They should bring in the type of rules we need in this House.
On this particular issue, I know how important it is to the civil servants to get all their papers out. But let me tell this House another little story. Even though an order in council went out in 1971 that we were going to have metric conversion, the civil servants who worked on this program so efficiently and thoroughly over the past seven years forgot to tell the government that they had to have legislation to make that possible. Last fall they rushed to the government and said, "Give us legislation." It was not until the last minute, just before Christmas, that they got it together. This legislation is going into effect tomorrow. The government does not consider it will have any trouble pushing it on the farmer. The railways

do not, and will not accept it. Parliament spoke last week. That bill, which all parties accepted in principle, is in committee. I am sure the government is smart enough now to accept the amendment that we proposed last week, will put it through and will take the rap, as we all should.
In conclusion, this move today not only shows the arrogance of a government too long in power, but shows a philosophy that is not suited for this country. I do not like to be bossed by the dictators on the left, or the dictators on the right. I certainly do not like to be bossed by the dictators who do not even sit in parliament. Mr. Speaker, this is one of those perennial debates which anyone who believes in democracy and our system of government is ready to oppose, whether he is on the government side or in opposition. Those in government today should oppose it because they will likely be in opposition before long. They should be prepared for that eventuality and support the idea of agreements between parties, rather than the use of force. It is true that this government has the right, because of its majority, to make the final decision.
Looking at legislation that has been passed over the last few months-in fact, years-there have been very few occasions when members of the government or of the opposition were smart enough to persuade the civil servants that something in an act should be changed. Therefore, it is almost assured that, with this government's present majority, this bill will be passed in exactly this way. This government did not have any input into the bill originally. Nor did it have any input at any stage in this House. However, it is not prepared to allow the opposition to make some changes. It would certainly shorten the debate if the government gave some consideration to the arguments being made by the opposition.
I listened with interest to the remarks of the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin). She stated that 41 tax returns involving rebates have been processed to this date. Big deal! I agree that is not a large number. However, these people are not entitled to rebates until after March 31. Therefore, it is not a very important consideration. It is also a fact that only 3 per cent of all returns are in by the end of February. Most of those ask for a rebate. The hon. member opposite makes a lot of noise. With the extra $4,000 he is being paid, he should think about some of our problems. If he wants to make loud noises, he should do that in caucus.
Where did you get your licence to prophesy?
Order, please. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) has the floor for the purpose of making a speech.
I may not have a licence to prophesy, but let me tell that loud-mouthed member that legislation would pass through this House a lot quicker if we were not given so many ombudsman bills.
"Omnibus".

Well, whatever the word is. There is no great rush about these budget bills. The government knew what it wanted when the budget was presented last May. Rather than throwing all these bill together, it would have been easier to process them if they had been separate bills for the retirement savings plans, the retirement pension plans and the child care plan. The government should have learned by now that it would be a lot easier if they did not throw in everything but the kitchen sink. It would make more sense to separate these bills. We could then make some progress.
I think the retirement savings program, which is relatively new in this country, could be introduced in a bill and those who are interested in that subject might pass it in a couple of days. Remember that this is not fair: it gives a lot more money to those who are making $20,000 and over than it does not those who are making $6,000 or $7,000; and also remember that those who are making $6,000 or $7,000 are paying for the gain of those who are making over $20,000. If you do not pay it one way, you pay it another. You are talking about money that is being raised to pay the taxes of this country. If you give more money to those earning a higher income than to those earning a lower income, then the latter pay for the benefits that the former get.
I think it would be reasonable to allow two to three days for a debate on the retirement savings plan. It can be said that we have had a pension plan for a long time and everybody understands it, and since there is no change in the pension structure perhaps the bill could be passed in a day and a half. As to the child care provision, there is considerable controversy about whether it provides any kind of equality at all to the people in this country. I think the Minister of National Revenue would probably agree, because she is a woman, that at the low end of the income structure women are in more desperate need of work than they are at the high end, and for that reason there is probably a greater need for child care for people with low incomes than for those with high incomes and much of the assistance will have to flow from the publicly-developed child care structures.
This is provincial. The $108 million is the amount people are waiting for in deductions.

That amount of money is the money that all taxpayers are paying to a few taxpayers who are able to get benefit from it. I suggest that if that were in a separate bill it could be passed in two or three days. All of that, and a lot of junk, is in the income tax bill. There are a lot of provisions in it and we have already allowed five days for it. The minister is saying we will get eight more hours. I think it is this type of

conglomerate bill that is unreasonable; and if it is not unreasonable, then the official opposition in the House is to blame because they agreed to Standing Order 75C. I should like to ask the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), who has a lot of experience in this field, a question. But would it not serve the members of parliament, and serve the process of law, much better if we were not to put bills before the House with some provisions which some members accept and others do not so that we get to the point where nobody knows what is acceptable and what is not.
I listened to the speech of one member from the official opposition and I do not know whether that party is for, or against, this bill. I am not sure that they know, either. I think the government should be more fair to the opposition. We have had several such bills, such as the bill on justice, this bill on income tax-

Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few moments to protest the move by the government to bring down the guillotine on the tax bill now before the House. I would not have spoken were it not for some of the unrealistic arguments that have been put forward on the other side. For example, the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) said that the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) should sit down and shut up because by speaking he was delaying the refunding of some $108 million to the taxpayers of this country. That is pure balderdash.
The same minister said that only 41 income tax forms had been filed to date, out of the millions of forms that have to be filed in this country. May I remind the House that the deadline on filing income tax forms is April 30, so we have a lot of time: we have three months to go. I know that many taxpayers in this country will not be getting refunds before some time in March, April or, indeed, May or June. It is a phony argument to say we have to impose closure on the House because we would be delaying refunds for thousands of
Income Tax
taxpayers. If the government wants to present arguments, the arguments should be credible. If it was serious about this bill and about the time factor, it would have made sure that the bill was brought to the House before this.
This bill is the result of the budget of last May 25, and the government delayed several weeks after the budget before the bill was brought before the House. Then, when parliament reconvened in the fall, the government delayed several weeks before bringing the bill back before parliament. When we came back a few days ago, the government had some other bills of a minor nature that they put on the order paper.
The bill before us today is one that we, as parliamentarians, should be discussing, studying and scrutinizing very carefully. It is a bill dealing with the taxation system. It is a system which is one of the more unfair systems of any of the industrialized countries in the world. Carter told us so many years ago, and many other people have documented the fact. We have just had a report from the National Council of Welfare, called the hidden welfare report, which says that literally millions and millions of dollars each year go out to people in this country in the form of tax write-offs, and so on. This bill will add to that. We know it will raise the limits for private pension plans. This bill would add to that: we all know that. It would raise the limits for private pension plans. It would end the surtax which was imposed on high income people to try to make them fight inflation along with the ordinary Joe.
As parliamentarians, these are the things we should be concerned about if we want to create a just society and a more egalitarian society. Instead, the government brings down the guillotine on this bill. That would not have had to be done if the bill had been introduced sooner. We could have had a good discussion. There did not have to be any acrimony. The government could have listened to the logical arguments of members of the opposition and of members in the progressive wing of the Liberal party. More equitable changes could have been made. For reasons like these, I cannot remain seated and not protest when the government brings in a motion to bring down the guillotine.
In a democratic parliamentary system-and the government House leader should be interested in this point-closure should not be invoked lightly or in a frivolous way. That should only be done with regard to a really serious piece of legislation which is considered an absolute must and which has to get through. It has to be a life and death type of situation-and surely this bill does not fit into that category. If the government is going to start using Standing Order 75C, closure, on small bills like this, I think the work of parliament will be slowed down and this place will become an even slower, more monotonous and more outdated institution than it already is.
One way to speed legislation through the House is by working with opposition parties and by making sure the opposition parties have a chance to air their points of view on things they feel are important. If the government would co-operate like that, I am sure it could expedite legislation through the

House. However, when the government brings in closure, it poisons the air of the House. A number of hon. members become angry, and angry members can hold up a lot of legislation for a long time. I know backbenchers will agree with me. It is in the government's own interest not to do things like this and not to antagonize hon. members over what is a relatively small piece of legislation, albeit a very important piece of legislation for many people in this country.
The government tried to put this bill through just before Christmas to give a large Christmas bonus to the wealthy people by increasing the limits for private pension plans, by increasing the limits for registered retirement savings plans and by ending the special surtax on high incomes. That is what the Liberal party tried to do. It tried to rush it through when people were not watching. It wanted to play Santa Claus to the wealthy people of this country.
Grow up.

The members of this party made up their minds not to go along with that, and before Chirstmas we stopped the bill. I do not buy that argument. The overwhelming majority of income tax returns have not even been processed.
They haven't even come in yet.
They have come in, but they can't be processed because you are delaying.

I suspect that many people have not yet even received their T4 slips, knowing the speed at which this government operates and knowing the Post Office of this country. If things are that far behind, why does the government want us to rush this bill through?
The taxpayers are behind.

The taxpayers are behind, partly because of the unfairness of the government. Little wonder the government is doing so poorly in the public opinion polls when it treats parliament, and opposition members who are here doing their work as well and as studiously as they can, with such arrogance, and when it tramples on all the good ideas which come from this side of the House. I am really glad I am not a Liberal backbencher, because I know they are expressing these ideas to their ministers, and they are being trampled upon. That is why so many of them are considering not running in the next election: they are disillusioned with the government.
I am glad the government brought in closure today, because that brings into the open the way it operates, the way it perceives people and the way it treats people. It brings it all out into the open and indicates to the Canadian people that this is a big, arrogant government-a Big Brother. By this action, the government is indicating that it wants to push

things through and trample on the rights of people just because it has to have its way. I see that my time is pretty well up.
Hear, hear!

However, I had to rise and say those words, not just on my own behalf but on behalf of many hon. members in the back benches of the Liberal party who sit there like muffled puppets on the end of a string and feel frustrated because of the actions of the powerful ministers who sit on the front benches. Liberal backbenchers know very well that they cannot speak their minds because they would be denying themselves promotion to parliamentary secretary positions or eventually to the cabinet or to the Senate. I know most of them want to follow the lead of hon. Jean Marchand and eventually end up in the Senate, because that is where all good Liberals want to end up. It is really on behalf of all those good Liberal friends of mine that I have made these few very relevant remarks this afternoon.
Mr. Speaker, I also want to say a few words about this motion under Standing Order 75C. I also want to speak on behalf of alienated Liberals from the three prairie provinces.
There are only three of them.

Liberal backbenchers cannot get the message through to those in the two front rows and those in the middle. They do not seem to have the courage or the guts to do so. If they do have the courage or the guts, they do not have the muscle to get messages through to the cabinet. If what they hear back home is meaningless to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), the government House leader and the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin), then I would be only too glad to assist those Liberals, because what the government is trying to do in this legislation is not meant to help most of the people of Canada.
The government has invoked Standing Order 75C, which it has the right to do under the rules, but it is doing so in the case of legislation which will help only about 30 per cent of the taxpayers of the country and the overwhelming majority- about 70 per cent-will reap little or no benefit. Those who have the lowest incomes will reap the least benefit from this legislation.
Much has been said about alienation in this country-not just in Quebec-and one wonders why there is alienation. People feel alienated when they find out, sometimes weeks, months or even years after the fact, that if they have an income of only $10,000 a year, a wife, two or three children and mortgages up to their eyeballs, they will reap benefits under this bill totalling close to $500 in 1977, but that the fellow who is in the $25,000 bracket will reap benefits of, would you believe, $1,156, give or take a few dollars here or there.
Under this bill, people in the $50,000 bracket-and that includes civil servants, cabinet ministers, union leaders and

corporate executives; a lot of people-will benefit by a little over $2,000. In the fight against inflation which the government has been waging, one would have thought that it would at least have had the decency to continue the idea that those who have can pay a little bit more for a little while longer should do so. But no, the government wants to relieve those on high incomes. For the government this is just another step on its way to the cemetery.
Mr. Speaker, no wonder there is alienation. This bill is one of the reasons-this unfair tax system which requires people at the lowest end of the income scale to pay a disproportionate share of the cost of running the country. Of course, there is nothing new about that: it has been chronic with old-line party governments in this country since year one.
The alienation is compounded almost weekly. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is liable to ask for a motion under rule 75C before this part of the session is much older. He got kicked in the head for wanting to hurt places like Halifax and St. John's, Baie Comeau and Quebec City, the Georgian Bay ports, the western grain producers and the flour milling industry of Canada. He got kicked in the head all last fall, and I am convinced that finally his colleagues persuaded the government to withdraw that clause from an earlier bill proposing government restraint. But I will be damned if the same minister did not bring the same provision back to the House in another bill.
Alienation is not peculiar to Quebec, Mr. Speaker. I do not know how many times the Minister of Transport has to be kicked in the head or how many times a brick wall has to fall on him. The trained seals and pacified sheep over there sit silent, but I hope they make some noise in their caucus. They certainly do not make it here. They drive people to wanting separation. There are a few in every part of the country who feel that way, and with the government's total lack of priorities they will continue to try to pass legislation that helps the wealthy and forgets about unemployment. They did not really implement their own anti-inflation program. They said the minimum increase in income should be $600 per year, but I do not see the old age pensioners getting that. That was not a priority; the priority was bulldozing various and sundry items through this House. This reminds me of a late, unlamented premier of Saskatchewan, Mr. Speaker, who proposed legislation about branding irons, chicken debeakers and turkey saddles at a time the province had the highest unemployment for years. The same thing is happening here.
While the official opposition may vote with this party in opposing the motion, I would have thought they would be stridently opposing the legislation as well. But I hear a strange silence from them. I can recall no objection from any member of the official opposition about a taxpayer with an income of $50,000 a year saving $2,000 under this bill, while somebody with a $5,000 income saves only $500 or less. 1 would have thought the official opposition would have wanted to reverse that table. Certainly, we New Democrats would like to reverse the child care provision. A family with an income of $10,000

The alienation continues, Mr. Speaker. It is not only because of the bill I mentioned earlier, stupidly introduced by the Minister of Transport with the consent of the government House leader. ti2 This past weekend I spoke in the riding of a Liberal member. That is because in areas of Newfoundland, in areas of northern New Brunswick, in areas of the Gaspe, in areas of northern Ontario, and in Cape Breton there just are no jobs.
When I apply for a disability pension on behalf of a constituent, I am astounded to get a letter saying the disability allowance is not available because the applicant can do light

work. Where is anyone to get light work in Cape Breton, northern New Brunswick, Newfoundland or the Gaspe, Mr. Speaker? The fact is that personal savings in Canada in the last three years have gone up. We do not need incentives for our people to save. Such arguments are false. My long-time friend, the deputy prime minister, recently made a speech after being awarded an honourary degree for his work concerning the reform of parliament. I was impressed by his speech. income distribution in this country, and less concerned about forcing through the House this legislation which will benefit the rich. When are the progressive elements of the Liberal party going to make the party truly liberal, instead of listening to its right wing?
The Conservatives.

Your present income distribution policies are hurting the people of Canada, and it should be obvious that they are hurting you, too. No wonder you will be thrown out in the next election, when you introduce bills like this.

After studying the bill, you can only come to one conclusion. Nothing focuses attention more on the inequalities in this country and on the welfare system which favours the rich than this sort of debate. In other words, the government does not want to debate the bill.

Mr. Claude-Andr£ Lachance (Lafontaine-Rosemont) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider a revision of the financial structure of the St. Lawrence Seaway, by remitting the interest carried over to date, by converting the loans which were made into holdings owned by Canada, and at the same time make provision for an increase in Seaway toll rates sufficient to cover annual operation costs and current capital expenditures, and also to provide the government with a return on its investment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I must confess that after all this confusion, it is somewhat difficult to gather one's thoughts and get into an argumentation on the subjet. Since I thought that the motion of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) would be called, I have had relatively little time to gather my thoughts. However, this subject has concerned me for some time. I remember, in particular, that last year the officials of the St. Lawrence Seaway Administration appeared before the Committee on Public Accounts and told something about their financial difficulties, especially in view of the somewhat peculiar financial structure of the St. Lawrence Seaway Administration and in particular in view of the decision made in 1970 by the American counterpart to our administration, that is the St. Lawrence Seaway Administration, American Section, to

remit interest outstanding up to 1970 and also to transform into assets capital expenditures on the American side.
In fact, I think it might be appropriate to give the background of the St. Lawrence Seaway and the reasons which brought both government levels to sign an agreement in 195455 to build this seaway which, as everyone knows, joins the Atlantic ocean to the Great Lakes by way of the St. Lawrence itself. Indeed, before the inauguration of the seaway, it was extremely difficult to move goods by ship since the St. Lawrence River did not lend itself to it. Anyway, the Welland Canal had been in operation for many years, which allowed small boats and shallow draught steamships to navigate on the Niagara River.
But it was decided that it might be preferable to dig a canal so that larger freighters could go directly from the Atlantic ocean to the Great Lakes and particularly to Lake Michigan and Lake Superior to avoid the transfer of cargo at Montreal or Quebec City harbours into smaller vessels that could negotiate the St. Lawrence above Montreal where there is not much water.
This agreement was reached at the two levels of government-American and Canadian-and it was decided then that a first amount of $350 million would be lent to the Canadian St. Lawrence Seaway Authority to begin work. This first loan of $350 million was spent between 1953 and 1959 to dig and build locks and all the necessary facilities.
Yet, the interests were obviously capitalized when the seaway became operational and the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority was supposed to start paying those interests which amounted to some $65 million.
We should not forget that when traffic projections and toll schedules were established initially the seaway was to be largely profitable and it was expected that it would repay the interest on the original loan and also the invested capital. Anyway, the Canadian government has always considered that this capital which has been, in the last seven years, invested in capital expenditures or real estate, was a liability, therefore an account receivable which has been left, in spite of several recommendations from several committees and directors of the seaway, in the liabilities of the seaway and therefore as an account receivable for the Canadian government.
Unfortunately we should recall that the initial forecasts as concerns the increase in seaway traffic, inflation, inflationary pressures which have, of course, affected the operations of the seaway, wages, and so on, have prevented the initial forecasts from becoming reality and we realized later that in spite of surpluses in its every day operations and the fact that it repaid regularly the interest, the seaway would never be able to refund the initial loan which was of $350 million as I said.
We must also remember that to accommodate larger freighters we had to invest up to $185 million to renovate the old Welland Canal, dredge it and develop existing facilities. Consequently, out of the total present debt of the St. Lawrence Seaway, $817 million, we must realize that about $500 million
January 31, 1977

are investments, holdings, real estate-locks, wharves, buildings, all the equipment necessary to the daily operations of the seaway-and the rest, about $318 million, are the accruing interests up to this day.
We must also remember that, as a joint American-Canadian commission is seeing to the enforcement of toll rates, the tolls can be increased only if there is a consensus between the two levels of government. Twice between 1960 and 1970, in 1964 and in 1967, studies showed that, because of inflation, the toll rates had to be re-examined and that an increase should be considered.
Unfortunately, both times the two levels of government could not reach a consensus and the rates stayed at their former level. On the other hand, in 1971 the Carr report made two main recommendations aiming first at a 10 per cent increase in the toll rates and the prescribed rates and at a reorganization of the financial and accounting systems of the St. Lawrence Seaway.
We must also remember that in 1970, as a result of similar problems faced by the American authority of the St. Lawrence Seaway, the American government had taken a momentous decision concerning the financial structure of their seaway authority. They had decided more particularly to capitalize capital expenditures already made. Evidently those expenditures were lower on the American side since they have only two locks. Nevertheless they decided to put what was considered as accounts receivable among the fixed assets of the American government.
On one hand, since interests were regularly accruing, they decided to pay off the entire debt and on the other hand, to provide that the American authority of the St. Lawrence Seaway should pay each year a fixed amount to reimburse the floating debt. Consequently the American sector now enjoys an extremely healthful financial condition and each year with its operating surplus it pays off the interests. On the other hand, its decision was not taken in spite of the urgent and pressing requests of various directors. 1 am thinking in particular of Messrs. Camu and Laurendeau. I could not speak for Mr. Chevrier, but in the annual report of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority for 1975, it was clearly indicated that he suggested precisely what is provided for in my motion, namely, and I quote from memory: " ... to remit the interest carried over and convert the loans which were made into holdings owned by Canada, and at the same time, make provision for an increase in Seaway toll rates sufficient to cover annual operation costs and current capital expenditures, and also to provide the government with a return on its investment."
As a matter of fact, the Canadian government did not follow up this matter for a very simple reason: because it is in the process of restructuring the main public corporations involved in transportation. I am thinking in particular of a bill which is now before the House concerning Air Canada and the CNR. The situations are somewhat similar in that the capital expenditures of those two corporations will eventually be converted into holdings owned by Canada and will no longer be accounts receivable. As a matter of fact, it is merely an accounting
St. Lawrence Seaway
fiction. It is now obvious that the St. Lawrence Seaway will not be able to meet its initial commitments, that it will not be in a position to repay the outstanding debt which now amounts to the astronomical amount of $819 million, that it will not even be able to repay the interests due, because it has not even been in position for three years now to cover its operation costs.
I have here the estimates for 1976-77, and the estimated revenues are $26.5 million while the estimated expenditures amount to about $36.5 million, for a $10 million deficit. This does not include the interest due for 1976-77 which amounts to $45 million. There is no question whatever of reimbursing one penny of the interests due, which means that the government will have to continue the fictional financing of the St. Lawrence Seaway since it is the creditor and loans and interests due are not recoverable through the seaway operations.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, my explanation might give the impression that the St. Lawrence Seaway is in a very unsound financial position and is not viable. In my opinion, it is a misleading conception of the situation. In fact, it is not possible to simply assess the St. Lawrence Seaway strictly in relation to its operation costs or its capital costs since it represents an asset, a tremendous economic advantage for Canada, providing a very convenient means of transportation for freight traffic between the Atlantic Ocean and the Great Lakes.
In any event, the tonnage keeps increasing ever since 1959, that is since the opening of the seaway and it is expected that this tonnage increase will continue during the next 15 years, at an average rate of about 2.5 per cent. In fact, Mr. Speaker, this tonnage passed from an average of 12 million tons during the years just before the opening of the seaway in 1959 to 57.6 million tons in 1973, a record year so far. In fact the increase in the Welland Canal itself is still more significant because similar increases pushed traffic up to 67.2 million tons in 1973.
Since then the Seaway Authority had all sorts of problems beyond its control: strikes, bad weather, problems in grain transportation; in short, things have improved gradually, the situation now seems better and the administrators are extremely confident that the increase will continue during the next 15 years.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, it is good to underline the great economic value of the St. Lawrence Seaway. It is worth just mentioning that the overall value of products carried through the seaway system was estimated at approximately $6 billion. Of course, this amount does not include the indirect benefits accruing to the shippers, the cost of commodities to the consumer and, of course, the expansion of international trade for Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I shall try to be brief but I simply want to explain to what extent it would be possible for the government of Canada to give back to the St. Lawrence Seaway a sound financial structure, which can be done without spending a single cent. It is strictly a bookkeeping operation similar to what the U.S. government did in 1970. As the directors of the St. Lawrence Seaway said themselves before the Committee

on Public Accounts, and this is the wording of my motion, Mr. Speaker, we would simply have to remit the interest carried over to date, namely about $318 million, and to convert the loans which were made originally, namely $500 million-$350 million for the St. Lawrence Seaway itself and about $200 million for the administration of the Welland Canal-into holdings owned by Canada, and at the same time-and this is for the past-put an end, once and for all, to the difficult situation in which they find themselves and provide for the future an increase in the seaway tolls sufficient to meet operating costs, for, as I said a while ago, this year the operating deficit will amount to some $10 million while, naturally, enabling the government, if the administration becomes sound, to make a return on its investments.
Mr. Speaker, I know this matter has been of concern to the government for some time now, and that it has been the subject of many a study. It must be understood that, though this is an accounting operation, it also fits within the wider context of the financial restructuration of the big state-owned transport companies. As I said before, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) tabled a bill in the House whose aim is precisely the organization of the financial activities of the CN and Air Canada. I feel it would be indicated to integrate the St. Lawrence Seaway into that policy; that would enable the seaway to have firm objectives in the future, and of course, it would reassure its users who really do not know what to expect, and I don't blame them. In fact, that may be one of the main problems of the St. Lawrence Seaway in view of its precarious financial situation; and there again, this in a fictitious way, since the Canadian government, in the final analysis, must finance it and cover its expenses, while the users, who do not know where they stand cannot really plan their future activities.
I therefore advocate, strictly, in my motion, a reorganization that is long past due, a reorganization that has proved itself in the American equivalent of the St. Lawrence Seaway, through namely, the remission of interest and capitalization of fixed assets; to allow the administrators in the future to make better plans for their financial activities, investments and capital expenditures, so that they can really do the job they are paid for, that is administrate a business which is highly vital, economically fundamental for the prosperity of eastern Canada, particularly for Ontario and Quebec, and also of course for the Maritimes. This business is also highly vital for western Canada since it allows grain from this region to be transported directly without having to pass through costly intermediaries en route to foreign markets. In short, Mr. Speaker, this is an operation which is needed and I strongly urge the House to accept this motion and recommend this restructuration.
