speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in the debate on this very important resolution. It is very current to our problems. This nation stretches some 4,500

miles across the breadth of the North American continent. We are in keen competition with our trading partner to the south and the rest of the industrial free world. We are in keen competition in the movement of raw materials and minerals to the third world countries. As far as our competitive position is concerned, more and more people are concluding that we are not able to compete with our major competitors in many ways. In analysing our own economy we can readily see that we have built up our costs. This has placed us in a very difficult non-competitive position with much of the free world, including our major competitor the United States. Transportation is a key factor. Transportation of goods for export and within Canada for consumption plays a part in the total cost, whether we are buying or selling a commodity, of our efforts to provide jobs and a standard of living comparable to what is expected.
The development of the United States was handled somewhat differently than our own. Their core of government engineers designed and built much of their transportation system. I think of their waterways in particular. The Mississippi is a tremendous waterway, providing cheap transportation for much of their export goods as well as those consumed in the United States. Their core of engineers deepened, broadened and extended the Columbia River to the point where tugboats and barges can move coal, grain and lumber a long way inland. There is no question about the cost of developing their waterways. They felt that by developing the Mississippi, Columbia and Ohio rivers, as well as many other river systems, they were building their country. There was no question of charging it all back and paying for it. This is one of our faults in Canada.
I can readily accept the first part of this resolution. However, I absolutely oppose the second part. It is time for the federal government to play a role in building this country, making the facilities available to all Canadians no matter whether they live in central Canada, western Canada or eastern Canada. In other countries the waterways have proven to be a major competitive vehicle in getting their products to the export market as well as distributing them within the country. This resolution suggests that everything should be paid back to the federal government. We have been obsessed with the idea of paying back to the federal government. It is the duty of the federal government to build this country so that Canadians can find jobs competitive with those around the world.
This is a great country, with a great potential. The shipping industry is one of those great potentials. We have talked about an industrial policy for years. What has this country launched upon? It launched its industrial policy upon an air industry. We do not have a large enough market to sustain the air industry in which this government has invested. It may be terrible to say that, but it is true.
We cannot compete with the air policy of the United States. France and Great Britain had great difficulty maintaining their air industries. However, there are some industries that lend themselves well to industrial policy. The shipping industry is one of those. We have, if not the longest coastline in the
January 31, 1977

world, certainly the second longest. There is great potential in our inland waterways. However, what do we see? There is discouragement with regard to our waterways. There is hesitancy and reluctance to make use of our natural shipping lanes and coastal lines. One aspect of our industrial policy should be the shipping industry. It should be encouraged, not discouraged. The railway industry is another. It, too, lends itself to this philosophy because of the great breadth of this country. It would complement an industrial policy.
What does this resolution suggest, particularly in its last part? It states the following:
... by converting the loans which were made into holdings owned by Canada, and at the same time make provision for an increase in Seaway toll rates sufficient to cover annual operation costs-
I think they should be sufficient to cover annual operating costs, and I do not object to that. It goes on:
-and current capital expenditures, and also to provide the government with a return on its investment.
This is the point I wonder about: are we as a government investing in Canada to have a return on our investment in so many dollars and cents, or will that return come to Canada indirectly? That is the question which we, as legislators, have to ask ourselves. Will we be satisfied to have that return come back to us indirectly, not directly as this motion suggests? I say that in the long run we, as Canadians, must be prepared to say we are satisfied with that return coming back to us indirectly, and we are confident that it will if we provide the vehicle or the avenue, whatever you want to call the St. Lawrence Seaway, for Canadian products to enter world markets.
What will the doubling of the St. Lawrence Seaway tolls do, and what will the doubling of the fees on the Welland canal do to the shipping industry on the St. Lawrence Seaway? I have here an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail on June 24, 1976, which reads as follows:
Federal proposals to increase tolls on the Welland canal would double the fees for many vessels moving through the Seaway system-
I want to stop here and make the point that everybody in the House and in Canada knows that vessels using the St. Lawrence Seaway are mainly Canadian vessels manned by Canadian sailors. By doubling the tolls we will be making those Canadians ships less competitive with their counterparts on the ocean lanes. The article goes on to read:
-the twenty-eighth annual Conference of the Canadian Water Resources Association in Toronto has been told.
John MacDonald, chairman of the Great Lakes Waterways Development Association, said in a speech prepared for delivery to the conference that the proposals would decrease the use of the Seaway and seriously affect the interests of western Canada.
"We are told that Ottawa intends to charge for use of the Welland the same tolls on bulk cargo as those now prevailing on the international Seaway," he said.
A group of people who have studied the St. Lawrence Seaway want to see it used to a greater extent than it is today. What would that do to Canadian ships? It would mean more jobs for Canadians. If we did not increase the tolls, it would
St. Lawrence Seaway
make Canadian goods more competitive with other goods in world trade, and it should make foreign goods in Canada cheaper for the Canadian consumer.
In my view it would be logical and it would make good sense for the government to say to the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, "We believe that you should charge tolls which would allow you to cover your costs of operation, but we do not expect you to pay an increase on the money we, as the Canadian government, have paid in the building of the St. Lawrence Seaway". I think that is a fundamental point.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) once said in the House of Commons that this would allow Americans to use the Seaway free of charge. I want to make the point that the Americans use the Mississippi and they use the Columbia. They have a tremendous network of inland waterways which assist that nation in moving its products to export, and around its own country for internal trade. These waterways are the cheapest form of transportation that a country has. They are our cheapest form of transportation.
Some 50 per cent or 60 per cent of tonnage on the St. Lawrence Seaway is made up of western grain, but the major portion of the remaining cargo is made up of iron ore which is made into steel, and steel means good jobs. Today steel in world trade is a very competitive commodity. Steel mills in central Canada are in keen competition with Japanese and American steel mills. The steel mill and plant operating on the east coast is in keen competition with steel mills in the United States and in central Canada. Yet we have before us a resolution which will increase the cost of doing business in this country.
There may come a day when we will say that we should pool a little money to build an additional waterway, and that perhaps the Seaway could pay a little bit back so that we will build an extension of the Seaway and deepen and lengthen the locks. Perhaps some time in the future when we place ourselves in a competitive position in world trade we will be able to do that, but I say to the House that now is not the time. We are in severe competition with other countries; there is a tremendous growth in unemployment in Canada and economists say that 1977 will be a difficult year. Also, cargo on the Seaway is carried solely on Canadian ships. The men who man the ships on the Seaway are Canadians.
The doubling of the tolls, even on the Welland canal, as the Canadian Water Resources Association stated in Toronto last year, may well double the costs of many vessels moving on the St. Lawrence Seaway. This would place us in a more difficult position than the one in which we find ourselves. In the remaining portion of the 1970's Canada will remain in keen competition with other nations, so now is not the time to adopt this resolution, particularly its latter half.
There is only one other point that I wish to make, and I think I would be remiss if I did not make it. If we double the tolls on the Welland canal unilaterally, we can expect some retaliation from the United States which might come in many different ways. For example, they could double their tolls on the Sault Ste. Marie locks. This would be detrimental to

St. Lawrence Seaway
Canadian shipping and would add to the cost of moving grain and other products through the St. Lawrence Seaway.
In 1976 we took action with regard to the beef industry which we in this party said would bring retaliation, but we were scoffed at. However, retaliation did come in one form or another. One only had to listen to the former U.S. secretary of agriculture, Mr. Butz, speak in Saskatoon a month ago to realize that retaliation was thought about and talked about by the United States government. Retaliation does take place, but whether it is visible and clearly seen by all is another thing. If we unilaterally double the tolls on the locks of the Welland canal we will be asking for retaliation. If we increase the tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway, we will only hurt ourselves in the long run.
We are making Canada less competitive and creating more unemployment, not just in the shipping industry, as I mentioned before, but also in the manufacturing industry, which wants to get its products out into that shipping lane. To put it bluntly, we are creating less revenue for the farmers of western Canada, and anyone who knows anything about western Canadian farmers knows that when they have a dollar they spend two to buy equipment which is manufactured in central Canada.
We turn off the whole economy with what I call this search for additional revenue, which is a method of taxation. That is really what the resolution means to me. It is a search for additional revenue by a money hungry government which already spent far more than it should have spent in 1974, 1975 and 1976. I would like to see the government reduce its demands for additional revenue for 1977, not search for more ways to raise revenues. I would like to see the government reduce the rabid expenditures which have taken place in recent years which have harmed the Canadian economy and which have helped to put us all into a very difficult competitive position. By adopting this resolution we would only find ourselves in a worse competitive position.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the hon. member who moved this resolution and to the most recent speaker, I have a few things to say about the general effects of the resolution, but I want to speak mainly about the Welland Canal. My constituency covers a good half of it, the important southern end. The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) was expounding on government expenditures. He should remember that we have cut down expenditures in every government department. That has been going on for well over a year, so I think his remarks can be overlooked because they are not very accurate.
As far as the Welland Canal is concerned, I do not think the remarks of the hon. member were correct on that either. For the last four years I have been talking about this with my constituents, and also with the members of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority. We cannot by any means say that all the ships and sailors on the St. Lawrence Seaway going through

the Welland Canal are Canadians. There is a huge number of salties. There is a fair number of American ships, and many Canadian ones.
What is carried through the Welland Canal which mainly affects Canada? It is mainly coal from the Lake Erie ports on the United States side, and iron, both from Thunder Bay and from Pennsylvania, but mainly from Thunder Bay and the north shore. Where do they go? They go to Hamilton. They supply the steel companies there, Dofasco and Stelco. A considerable amount of grain is shipped several times a year in large quantities, but a great amount of grain is shipped past us to Toronto, to Montreal and to Maritime ports by rail. When we talk about increasing the tolls and about the cost of shipments through the Welland Canal, we are really talking about so many cents per ton of coal. According to the Seaway Authority, it decided to apply four cents to the cost of shipping each ton of coal. I think some people do not remember how much the price of coal has gone up. It costs about $52 or more per ton, and four cents on $52 is very little.
With regard to steel, the same logic applies. A few cents on a ton of iron ore do not affect the competitiveness of our Canadian manufacturing firms at all. Similarly, the very few cents added to the cost per bushel of transporting wheat is almost negligible, and we have no trouble disposing of our wheat. In fact recently we sold another huge order to China.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my party has long taken the position that something like the St. Lawrence Seaway is a public work for the national good. It is a part of a national transportation system which benefits the nation as a whole. In fact it is an instrument of national policy. I want to tell the hon. member who moved this resolution that at least one part of his resolution would discriminate further against producers, shippers and exporters in different parts of the country because of where they happen to live, our geography and our climate.
I think there is no disagreement that the debt, and the interest thereon of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority should be taken over by the government of Canada. That would signify the total public ownership of the St. Lawrence Seaway,
January 31, 1977

and the cost of that debt should be born by the nation as a whole and not just by the users. I hope there is little or no argument about that concept anywhere in this House, and I hope my good friends on the government side will remind the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) that this is one area where his idea of user pay should not be allowed to take effect.
I want to remind the hon. member who moved this resolution that making provision for an increase in Seaway toll rates sufficient to cover annual operation costs and current capital expenditures is just not acceptable. Current and future capital cost expenditures should be borne by the government.
I see some inconsistency in this resolution. Current and future capital cost expenditures should be borne by the nation as a whole, just as the hon. member proposes in the earlier part of his resolution, but original capital costs and interest debts should also be assumed by the country as a whole. I do not know how the hon. member can have it both ways. Providing the government with a return on its investment is just nonsense. Something which is a public utility and a requirement is an asset to the nation as a whole. I do not know of any town, village or city looking for returns on their investments in sewer systems, water systems and highways. The St. Lawrence Seaway falls into the same category.
The last point in the resolution is totally unacceptable to most people in this country. The St. Lawrence Seaway is one of the main transportation routes in our nation. It is a benefit. The nation as a whole shares the cost. The nation as a whole can and should carry the cost of transportation in every part of the nation and in whatever form, whether ferries and causeways in the Atlantic provinces, a waterway like the St. Lawrence Seaway, or ports like Churchill and Prince Rupert. If these are to be operated not only on the basis of paying the costs of operation but recovering the cost of all capital, interest, and a return on investment, only the rich could travel. We would export little and we would have trouble importing because people would not be able to pay the price of goods.
Surely the fact that ships are energy efficient means that we should promote greater use of them in this country. Grain producers must have low cost water transportation if we are to remain in competitition with other grain exporting nations.
In his remarks the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) spoke of doubling the tolls. An article which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle Herald on June 4 last reported Mr. Paul Normandeau, president of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, as telling the Public Accounts Committee that tolls would have to be five times higher than their existing levels in order to put the St. Lawrence Seaway on a paying basis. Now my hon. friend would have us accept a resolution that would not only put it on a paying basis but would give the government a return on its investment. There is no way we can accept that, Mr. Speaker.
I would remind hon. members that Canadian cargoes move toll free through the United States locks at Sault Ste. Marie. I agree with the hon. member for Crowfoot that if we were to
St. Lawrence Seaway
increase our tolls there would of course be retaliatory action. This would be bound to have an effect on Alberta coal moving to Ontario. I suggest that the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton) check with Ontario Hydro and Ontario consumers to see how they would like that. It also means that grain shipments, about ten million tons a year, could be diverted to United States ports.
This is a public utility and it could operate at cost to the user. The capital cost and interest cost should be assumed by the nation as a whole. Those who advocate it should operate with a return on investment to the government should remember that the government is the people of Canada. This facility is meant to function for the welfare of the people of Canada, as are a lot of other facilities.
My hon. friend across the way speaks of international shipping. How many international ships would use the St. Lawrence Seaway if these tolls were imposed? They would use United States ports.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture represents agriculture from the Atlantic to the Pacific. In a brief submitted to the government last September, the federation opposed any increase in the tolls although they supported that part of the hon. member's resolution which proposes the government should take over interest charges. Their brief reminds us that the United States government absolved those responsible for their portion of the St. Lawrence Seaway of all past, present and future capital and interest costs. It would seem to me we can do no less.
The brief also had this to say:
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture opposes any increase in tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway, and further recommends that the capital debt and interest accumulated thereon be assumed by the Government of Canada.
The interest and debt amounts to something over $800 million, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that if the government moves anything as horrendous-that is the correct word-as a closure motion, it ought to have some justification for it, and the justification which has been put forward by spokesmen for the government is that until Bill C-22 passes income tax rebates in 1976 cannot be processed.
It is important to consider statistics. They show that the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue normally processes 3 per cent of all tax returns by the end of March, and we say that this bill would pass by then in any event. More significantly, we argue that certain rebates can be made within the authority of legislation passed so far. After all, Bill C-21 to do with the excise tax deals with sales tax exemptions which relate to the same May, 1976, budget.
As I said when speaking about tax returns, on average only 3 per cent of all such returns are processed by mid-March, only 20.2 per cent of the total are processed by mid-April, and 36 per cent by mid-June. Not until mid-August will, say, 92.3 per cent of all tax returns have been processed.

My party has shown strong determination in opposing passage of this measure; unfortunately, since there are only 16 of us in the House of Commons it is most unlikely that we could hold up this legislation, much as we are determined to try, long enough to interfere significantly with the processing of tax returns. I therefore suggest that the government is being less than honest with Canadians when it says that it must impose closure in order to help the taxpayer, particularly the little taxpayer.
I have had a number of letters from irate citizens who have at least $11,000 tucked away in savings. They are angry with me for opposing this bill. They want to add to their savings and they do not want to pay taxes.
I say that the government is not justified in bringing in closure. Its two grounds for the motion, namely, that passage of the bill is necessary because it will help certain people and that it cannot pay rebates unless the bill passes, are without foundation. Therefore, it is scarcely justified in moving the closure motion. I think the government should be thoroughly ashamed of itself for the less than honest manner in which it has placed this matter before the country.

Mr. Speaker, we oppose this motion. We believe firmly that the use of closure is the wrong way to run a democratic parliament. I agree with the remarks made by one or two members this afternoon on the government side of the House, that we must find ways to apportion our time and use it sensibly as among various kinds of legislation. Some pieces of legislation are important and deserve considerable debating time; some are unimportant and ought to be dealt with quickly.
What bothers me about the present method of using closure is that it is a case of giving in to the idea that there is no way to work out our timing arrangements on a sensible basis. Therefore every time we use closure we put off the day when we shall find a better way. So, Mr. Speaker, because we think it is wrong to apply closure to a bill as contentious as this one, and because we think that the use of the closure rule delays the finding of a better and more co-operative way to run the House of Commons, we strongly oppose this motion. I say this as one who has often advocated a sensible apportionment and allocation of our time. I think it can be done. I think we can start a session with a clear indication of what is to come before the House, and with an agreement as to which measures are important and deserve debating time, and which measures can be dealt with quickly. But so long as we have a government which refuses to give us the session's program in advance and relies on the present ad hoc, helter-skelter way of doing things, we shall have a parliament which does not deal with its business in a business-like and appropriate way.
As a member of this House I have seen a good many applications of the closure rule-the old one as well as the new one-and I can say that every time it is used it creates feelings of ill will; and, worse, this procedure prevents us from working out a sensible way to deal with the business of the House of Commons.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of the clauses to which we take exception in terms of the disproportionate benefits it provides to some people in comparison with others. I have a table which I would like to read in connection with how the benefits occur with regard to child care expenses. In considering child care expenses we find that there are many tables here dealing with who benefits and who does not. There is a table in conjunction with registered retirement savings plans and child care for two children. If income is $10,000, the saving is $210. The disability deduction, which is one of the highly touted aspects of this bill, is $275. We are not complaining that these savings at that income level should not take place, but if we go on to higher incomes, for example, $50,000, the saving is doubled. In the case of a registered pension plan the saving is $430. In the case of an RRSP the saving is $645.
Using that income, in the case of child care where two children are involved the saving is doubled. The saving is $430. It seems to me that these things should be organized in such a way that the saving is equal. If in fact the saving is to be $210 at the $10,000 level for the registered pension plan, or $210 in the case of the child care plan, it should be the same for everyone right across the board, and we object to the fact that the saving is larger with higher incomes. That is the feature all the way through the various aspects of the bill which we find so offensive.

This is a point about which the hon. member's colleagues have been making a great deal. The response is that on the other hand the tax payable at the various levels indicated is upped as income is progressively

greater. It is true that there is a larger reduction in tax as you go up the income scale. On the other hand, there is a very much greater absolute tax payable.

This is the kind of thing we hear when we talk about progressive income tax in this country. They say lower the rates because they are too onerous. Then the minister comes along and says that we have a progressive income tax, and look what the rates are. What we are saying is that this is only one example. There are many more examples which we have put forward. Every time a deduction is introduced which makes it possible for people with higher incomes to get greater benefits from registered retirement savings plans, child care deductions and even disability deductions, the progressiveness of the income tax system is reduced. This is what is being done all along in our income tax system as a result of these various deductions. In fact the system is not nearly as progressive as the minister makes it out to be.
I just have to point out to the hon. gentleman that the percentage change remains the same all the way up.

Mr. Chairman, what is the argument of the government against a tax credit arrangement? The minister says that the percentage remains the same ail the way up. That is true, but the amount does not remain the same all the way up. In some cases the amount is considerably more than in others. If we were to use a tax credit out of tax payable and if we set a fixed sum, that would be the amount of a child care deduction. It would be an actual amount. It would apply to the rich the same as it would to the poor. It seems to me that when we do things on a sliding basis, that means that at the high end those who need it least get the greatest advantage, and this has to be paid by everyone. That is the amount the government does not get in taxes. Therefore everyone pays it, and those who need it most do not get the most advantage out of it. If this were calculated on the basis of a delayed tax, a deferred tax, or a tax which would be set at a fixed amount and the amount payable from the income tax were taken off, then this would be fair and it would also be in proportion to need.
Using the amount of $300 as an example, this sum would represent a higher proportionate amount to the poor than it would to the rich. It would be a very small proportion of the taxable income of those earning $20,000. In fact, it might cost them money because it would become income. On the other hand, at the lower end it would have quite an influence because it would be deducted directly from tax.
I would be interested to know why the Minister of Finance has not given some consideration to this more equitable proposal. It is being used now in Ontario with regard to the Ontario proportion of income tax both for the elderly and for farm properties. Both of them are in the form of a deferred tax. I see no reason why we should not at least consider this, because the minister must agree that what we are doing in each of these instances is providing a great deal more benefit at the top end of the tax structure than we are at the bottom. Every dollar deducted at the top end is considerably more-

Mr. Chairman, in percentage terms it is equal. There is an inequality in the income tax structure but it is in the upper bracket, not the lower bracket. In percentage and absolute terms, the more you get the more you pay. This is done by way of deduction rather than giving a tax credit. It is regarded as a deduction available for certain people in the work force-primarily women, but also a single parent man. In order to earn income, if these people have dependent children they have to make arrangements for day care facilities. In that sense it is regarded as a sum expended for family purposes so that the taxpayer may be free to earn income.

Would the minister not agree that where we are setting up day care centres as are other segments of government, which are usually operated in a community structure where it is absolutely necessary to have this kind of care so that family may have enough money to get by on, that the need becomes greater at the low end of the income scale rather than the top end? The minister is correct in saying it is a progressive tax structure and that the rich pay more than the poor on a percentage basis, but would he not agree that there is more left over at the top end than at the bottom end?
In the example given to us, suppose the child care deduction were eliminated and replaced by a tax credit of $350 per child, for the woman whose earned income was $6,000 this would mean a $93 reduction in her tax bill. Instead of the $257 tax saving she now receives from the deduction, she would have her taxes reduced by $350, a difference of $93. The $20,000 a year woman would have her tax bill increase by $30 since the present tax deduction gives her a saving of $380, but the credit would only give her a saving of $350.
It seems to me we are interested in the low end of the scale particularly in those subsidized communities where a large percentage of people depend on two incomes and even the combined income is not very high. The tax credit would bring more relief on a percentage basis than it would the person at the top end of the scale, no matter what the physical amounts

Mr. Chairman, as indicated by my colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge, the minister seems to be arguing the case that income tax is set up in a progressive way so that the higher the income, the higher the percentage of tax. That is theoretically true, but every special provision we put into the act, such as this one, is another step toward destroying the very progressivity about which the minister spoke so favourably.
What do we see when we look at the child care provision? A large number of married women in Ottawa work, and I am sure every member knows some of them who have quite high qualifications. According to the income tax tables for this year, those who make between $20,000 and $25,000 per year will be taxed at 31 per cent on their taxable income. The minister is now proposing that $1,000 spent on child care should be exempt from income tax, which means that such a woman will save between $300 and $350. But her secretary, who is probably earning $8,000 or $9,000 per year, will pay 20 per cent tax on her taxable income and not save even half of what her boss does.
This provision does what the Carter commission pointed out years ago-it takes one more step toward destroying the progressivity about which the minister spoke. I see the minister shakes his head. I would be glad if he could explain how our argument is in error.
It seems to me that we should not be moving toward provisions which give people a legal method of avoiding income tax, but that we should be moving to eliminate these loopholes and special provisions. To a great extent they are used on behalf of people in the upper income bracket, or self-employed people, and are of little or no use to the ordinary working person on a low wage.

Mr. Chairman, I would make the point again that, of course, as the progressivity of the tax goes up you have the same relative percentage all the way up. It does not alter that, except as you top out, at that point some of the higher income does not get the same benefit it otherwise would if the expenditure goes above $1,000 per year. There is progressivity in percentage terms. Of course this is of more value in the higher of the two categories, but in percentage terms the relativity is the same.
The hon. member for Timiskaming says we should reverse the order and have declining benefits the more tax you pay.

The point I am trying to make, which has been made by many others, including the National Council of Welfare, is that we ought to be directing our attention either toward remodelling income tax along the present lines, or to some form of negative income tax. The aim would be to put money into the hands of people at the bottom end of the income scale rather than people at the top.
We have said many times that everything we have done over the last 25 years has led to the position we are in today where the bottom one fifth of income earners are getting a smaller percentage of the gross national product than they were 25 years ago. They are getting less than 4 per cent of the gross national product, whereas the people in the top group are now getting about 42.5 per cent of the gross national product. The kind of proposals the minister has put forward in this bill, along with other government proposals, have led to the present situation with which my party disagrees completely.

Mr. Chairman, I reinforce the invitation of the hon. member for Winnipeg North, particularly since we are debating this bill under a time allocation order. Backbenchers opposite should not be reluctant to stand up and present their ideas. Normally they are kept in line by their Whip who says they can yell from their seats but that they should not take up the time of the House.
It is clear, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North pointed out, that the efforts of the federal government and other levels of government to redistribute wealth have failed. While governments transfer money to lower income people through programs like the old age pension, guaranteed income supplement, family allowances and other government programs on the one hand, they give benefits and allowances of the kinds contained in the present bill to the better off, on the other. What the left hand gives the right hand takes away, and to that we object.
Let me give some examples. Most of us favour women's liberation. We think it is long overdue that women should be given equality in the eyes of the law. Unfortunately most of the benefits of the women's liberation movement are enjoyed by women of the middle and upper income brackets; poor women get few of the benefits, despite all the pitches you hear about women's liberation. How does that relate to the present legislation? This bill would allow women who do not want to stay home to work and deduct up to two thirds of child care expenses from income. In raising my argument I am not

saying that the law discriminates as between women. Circumstances in life can militate against certain women and the law is not taking those into account.
How do women at low income levels who go to work arrange for the care of their children? They do not send their children to child care centres or fancy nursery schools. They cannot afford those expensive luxuries. Generally a neighour or relative looks after the children. That is how women at lower income levels arrange for the care of their children during the working day. The fact is, at that level, you are not going to get receipts which you can present to the government for claiming a deduction. That is a fact of life, as anyone will attest who knows how people at the lower income level live.
But the people who will avail themselves of the deductions in this bill can avail themselves of all sorts of fancy schools, be they language schools or nursery schools. Those women will get the real benefit of the bill. I am talking of women who start bringing up their children from the age of three or four to be part of this society's elite; those women make sure that our present class distinctions continue. And that is what this bill is all about.
I know the minister is not inexperienced in dealing with constituents. His constituency contains more than one class of constituent, and he deals with all sorts of people in his constituency. He knows that the child care of the better off is different from the child care of the poor. This legislation, by its very nature, is designed to help the better off.
Let me touch on arguments regarding the progressive nature of our income tax system. I do not quarrel with the minister when he says that he is trying to maintain equity under the income tax system. I would not quarrel with the minister if the present income tax system were equitable and the programs associated with it were closing the gap between the rich and the poor. But how can he argue that inequality breeds equity? Really, that is what the minister is arguing. He is saying that he wants to maintain the present system of equity. We say that existing so-called equity is not worth a darn. It is widening the gap between the rich and the poor.
We do not favour the present sort of proposals which do nothing to make the income tax system more equitable. We say that the income tax system can be made more equitable if the government pays a tax credit, that is to say, if it pays the same amount to those at the lower end of the income scale that it makes available to those at the upper end. In that way it could make the income tax system somewhat more fair. That is the kind of equity for which we stand, in contrast to the kind of equity which the minister has put forward.

Mr. Chairman, I will not add to what the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge just said, but I should like to raise the matters he raised in the form of a question to the minister. I suppose one could argue that the present income tax system would be equitable if you were to treat everything in the market system in the same way, as being of equal value. Under such a system the government, through its progesssive income tax-I will not argue how progressive our

present income tax system really is, because I do not think it is progressive at all-would not say to Canadians that it prefers spending on automobiles as opposed to spending say, on bibles or other consumer goods. Under such a system one could argue that the government is taking a neutral position. But when the government provides incentives through its tax system and says, "We want you to spend money on child care or registered retirement savings plans," and so on, it is, by definition, making a value judgment. In other words, the state wants to encourage that kind of spending. On the other hand, if we are concerned about equality in society, should we not proceed on a direct grant basis, as my colleagues argued, to ensure that the tax system treats all people with equality? Would that not be better than the present income tax structure of this country?

Mr. Chairman, perhaps our viewpoint is somewhat different. We are recognizing under the tax system that people in the community, make financial contributions with regard to pensions for retirement, RRSPs, and child care expenses, contributions for which they are out of pocket and for which, reasonably, there should be some recognition in the tax they pay. I do not pretend for a moment that there is equality between all taxpayers. There is a fundamental assumption which is not obviated by the tax system, or by the income system within the community, namely, that some people are making more than others. We are saying, indeed, that there is not equality between taxpayers, because the higher you go up the income scale the more tax you pay, and you pay a greater percentage of your income in taxes. The hon. member is right in one respect. Even having applied those factors you still have more left in hand. But the money left in hand does not initially come from the tax system but from a whole variety of different circumstances in which people find themselves in the community.
I suppose, not intending to carry the hon. gentleman's argument to the extreme, I can refer to the United Kingdom taxation system where, in Canadian terms, at a relatively low level in the taxation system taxation takes away any additional earned income. In terms of incentive I would think on the whole it is in our interest to continue to leave substantial incentive out there for some people whom the hon. member might not regard as great contributors to the community, but also for a great many people with respect to whom he would concede are making contributions by their talent and otherwise and who are rewarded by a greater return on income. So there is a basic equality there. I suppose the hon. member would take more away in tax from those further up the income scale, but we would still leave them with more in the end.

The minister has replied to one aspect of the question, one upon which I really did not want to concentrate, namely, whether the income tax structure is sufficiently progressive-is there a certain point at which one should increase the amount one must pay. I should like him to deal with the question.

Let us assume there is a particular schedule of progressivity in the income tax structure and the democratic government of the day decides that certain goods and services, for example, the provision of day care facilities, are important and therefore should be encouraged by the state. If the government makes such a decision, does it not make a lot more sense to provide for these things directly as opposed to providing for them through the tax structure?
Consider, for example, the present measure providing for child care allowance. In terms of tax benefit the average person earning $10,000 a year, with two children, receives a benefit of $200, but a person earning $100,000 with two children, receives a benefit amounting to $470. What I am asking the minister is this: instead of attaching benefit for day care to the income tax structure as such, would it not be a lot better to leave it alone in this respect and to take a figure somewhere in between, say, $310, and make sure it goes as a direct payment to all taxpayers, or, indeed, to people who do not pay taxes because their income is not sufficiently high, but have a need of day care facilities? Is it not better for the state to involve itself in actions it believes to be desirable and pay for them directly, rather than using the tax system to pay for the service in such a way that the rich inevitably benefit more than the poor?

The hon. gentleman seems to be suggesting that instead of tax deductions we should make a transfer payment to individuals from the public treasury. I think there could be some debate about the wisdom of doing this. One thing is clear. Very likely the apparatus at government level for operating the transfer system and deciding who was to get payments and who was not, would be more expensive than the operation of the present tax system.

Mr. Chairman, under the present law certain taxpayers, working mothers, are allowed to deduct the actual cost of child care up to an annual maximum of $1,000 a year-as my colleague points out, the family maximum is $4,000 a year-provided the amount claimed does not exceed two thirds of a taxpayer's earned income for the year. According to the report issued by the National Council of Welfare, in 1974 child care deductions, which at that time had a maximum set at only half the present rate, cost the government of Canada over $29 million, so it is obvious that if we increase the amount to $1,000 per person as is now proposed, we are talking of an amount of money in the neighbourhood of $60 million.
I attended the annual convention of the Manitoba New Democratic Party this past weekend where there was a long and pretty acrimonious debate because many delegates felt that the provincial government was not putting enough money into day care centres. In explaining the position of the government, the premier agreed that the government was not putting in enough money, but argued that the amount spent by the government had gone up from almost zero three or four years ago to something in the neighbourhood of $3 million to $4 million for this coming year.
Since most of the $60 million goes to women in the middle and upper income brackets, it seems to me that we would accomplish a great deal more if, instead of giving these tax credits which the National Council of Welfare has indicated will probably cost the treasury $60 million, that amount were better spent in larger contributions to provinces which have already set up day care centres and want to expand them, or to provinces which want to set up day care centres. I wish the minister would give some thought to this.

If you ask yourself who benefits from this, who needs the help the most, you quickly would have to come to the conclusion that the people who need help the most are that group of people which is probably the largest group on welfare, the single parents. Very often there are complaints that they are on welfare, but this is often because they have a child. It is the largest single group on welfare. The greatest thing we can do in terms of getting these people off welfare and giving them a chance to go to work and realize an opportunity is to provide some service for them.
These are not the kind of people with the skills of those who earn a great deal of money. Anything we can give them through the income tax system in the way of a tax deduction or tax benefit is a waste of time. Chances are they will not earn enough money to be able to take advantage of it. Even if they get some money that puts them into a taxable bracket, the very regressive nature of this system tends to be less favourable for them than for people with higher skills and in a better position to get the money for the work they do.
The minister is responding in a way that often happens with these income tax systems. In other words, you start off with a system and you add a little bit of this and a little bit of that. You get pressure from one group or another. You say that in the next budget you will tack on a little piece for them, "do not get too upset with us." The party with which the minister is associated tends to be more inclined to look for the swingers, the middle and upper-income groups. He obviously has to be in some struggle to keep them happy.
A few years after the great Carter report when we tried to simplify the tax system, we keep having these things added. They not only complicate the tax system but increase its regressive nature. It gives little bits and pieces. We wonder why the distribution of income over all these years has really not been effective in any significant way. It is because of this kind of patchwork approach.
Getting back to the question of what should be done about the problem of child care, obviously something should be done. It reflects an absence of really looking at the problem and saying there is a child care problem.
There are a lot of people who should be helped if they want to go to work. They should be helped with child care expenses. What is the best way of doing it? Rather than coming up with this bitty thing that in fact keeps the middle-income people somewhat happy and sort of responds to the clubwoman type

of request, the minister should reconsider the government's attitude toward child care centres.
If the government is prepared to forgo this kind of revenue in the tax system, it should be prepared to use this amount of revenue which is significantly fairer and more effective than the measure before us today.

Mr. Chairman, I listened carefully to the minister's response. I appreciate the reasons he gave. They reflect government policy and also the reasoning of his officials. I consider the minister to be a pretty decent guy who thinks about and considers ordinary people. Why would he countenance this kind of program rather than fight for a program that would give a $470 tax saving to someone at the low end of the tax scale with a $10,000 income and only a $200 tax saving to the one at the $100,000 end of the income scale? Why, in the name of decency if nothing else, will he not do that?
Don't tell me the clause cannot be reworded to do that very thing. His officials, two of them here now, could work out a scale or formula that would reverse the position for the working mother who earns $7,000 or $8,000 a year as a waitress or stenographer so that she would get the maximum tax saving. Probably her whole income tax of $500 would be returned. The working mother in the $20,000 or $30,000 bracket would get less of a tax saving. If there is such a thing as a working mother in the $100,000 bracket, which I doubt, she would only get a $200 tax saving. Surely to God that is the decent thing to do.
I was hoping that some of my colleagues in the official opposition would have something to say about that tonight, because they have been the greatest motherhood party since last February. I was hoping someone would get up, but do you know what they think of child care? They are watching Evel Knievel on TV.
I did not know he was on now.

What is the stand of the official opposition on decent child care facilities? I had hoped the hon. member for Fundy-Royal, who has done some pretty good things about day care centres and child care, would have something to say, but he has been bloody silent tonight. The Tories would not even help force the vote so the Liberals would have to bring in closure.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Why watch TV; we have you here?

I ask not only the minister but the official opposition if they would not prefer to see the low income working mother get the maximum tax saving and the high income working mother get the minimum tax saving? That is what I would like to know.

Mr. Chairman, I wish the Minister of Finance would answer the questions posed by my colleague who just sat down. I would like to join my colleague in asking
January 31, 1977

where the official opposition is on this measure. I find it extraordinary that on one of the most significant parts of a tax bill that affects in particular average and low income people in Canada, the Conservative party in the House of Commons has had not one word to say. When they get around to policy development, their leader asks a man by the name Reuben Baetz, who is head of the Canadian Council of Social Development, but I understand he has been reluctant to give them advice. Perhaps he sees how cynical they are. I hope he reads the record of today's debate and finds out that the official opposition had not one word to say on this important measure.

Mr. Chairman, I was interested to hear the argument used by the National Council of Welfare on income tax systems, and I was particularly interested in their statement on the unfairness of some of the sections of the income tax law. I am sure that many Canadians will be very interested in this.
It may well be that the reason why more Canadians are not interested in day care centres and the ancillary facilities of day care work stems from the fact that this government does not want extra women in the labour market.
I went to a Manpower Centre in my own area a couple of weeks ago because I was obsessed with the idea that the figures which are available for employment do not meet the criteria that I would set, and in fact they are considerably below them. I asked whether there would be enough women in the area to fill the 300 vacancies available at a factory close by. An official said there were about 300 women listed at that Manpower Centre. I asked whether all those women would be able to work in that plant making jeans. He said that no, of course they would not, that there would be no trouble getting 300 women to work in that plant, but only 100 would be from his list. This means that in any particular field there might be four or five times as many women available for work as are registered. One of the reasons for that is the fact that if you have a very low income you have to get your neighbour or your mother-in-law to look after your baby when you go out to work. So these women agree to do the work of baby sitting for reasonable wages so long as they do not have to give receipts. They are not interested in the work if they have to give receipts because they do not want to get their husbands in trouble with their income tax forms. They are not interested in making that income otherwise. If they can get that income under the table without receipts, they will take the work.
Let me say for the edification of the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin that I had the opportunity to visit a country not long ago, a country to which Canada is giving considerable aid for development. One of the things on which they are spending a large amount of money is the development of day care centres in conjunction with their industrial projects. In fact every housing unit they build is connected to a day care centre. They believe it is absolutely essential for low income people to have two incomes per family, and to make that possible day care centres are necessary.
Surely the Minister of Finance, who comes from an area where many residents are in desperate need of day care centres
Adjournment Debate
and who leave their children in less than satisfactory conditions when they go out to work, must be sympathetic to the argument put forward by my colleague who said that this measure will mean a reduction of tax revenue for the federal government of about $60 million which could be invested in day care centres in conjunction with the municipalities and provinces. This would be of much greater benefit to the people in need of day care assistance than this kind of exemption which we believe, perhaps wrongly, is of greater benefit to the tax structure itself than to people at the lower end of the income scale.
I hope the minister will give some consideration to transferring to his colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, this money in lieu of the tax exemption so that we can build day care centres, and so that we do not find that a country which is much less progressive and developed than ours, and certainly much poorer than we are, does more in the area of social assistance than we do by building day care centres for those who need to work.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
Progress reported.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-COW-CALF SUPPORT PROGRAM-REASON FOR REDUCED PAYMENT TO PROVINCES WHICH HAVE PROGRAMS
AGRICULTURE-COW-CALF SUPPORT PROGRAM-REASON FOR REDUCED PAYMENT TO PROVINCES WHICH HAVE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the topic I want to pursue tonight is the cow-calf program, and I see the parliamentary secretary is here. One could describe the federal cow-calf program in the language of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) himself as being a load of bull. It is too little, too late; it discriminates against small producers, and it discriminates against provinces that set up continuing stabilization programs when the federal government refused to do its job.
The program allocates less to cover the whole country, $70 million, than Alberta and Saskatchewan budgeted for their 1976 programs, $72 million. The pay-outs are expected to be about $30 per cow less than the $50 Alberta and Saskatchewan were paying under the 1976 program, and will cover fewer cows.
At a meeting with the Minister of Agriculture in December the provincial ministers were led to hope that the federal plan would cover 1976 as well as 1977. That has not materialized. As with all other federal stabilization programs, the plan is not

January 31, 1977
Adjournment Debate
indexed to cover all costs of production. Ninety per cent of the five year average stabilization level will not come near to covering the producers' losses.
The payment set-up works against small producers by deducting the first five cows and then paying on 70 per cent of the remaining herd. Naturally this means that the small producer gets paid on a smaller percentage of his herd than a producer at the maximum 100 head. All this does is save the federal government a bit of money. If the federal government really wanted to exclude hobby farmers, it could have set a minimum cow herd and paid on the whole thing.
The government is only paying 70 per cent because it is assuming an 85 per cent calf drop. That means the producer gets no support at all for the cows that he breeds and feeds and on which he comes up a loser. However, the really foolish feature of this program is the additional 15 per cent exemption for herd replacement. If the government wants to end the depletion of the cow herd, which is going on very rapidly and which by mid-1977 may see us back to 1971 beef crisis levels, the way to encourage producers to build herds is not to reduce payments that may keep some of them operating until the market picks up as predicted.
In Saskatchewan, for example, there was a record cow slaughter in 1976 as 202,000 cows went to the slaughter yards-that is double the normal rate-and at that time the same pattern held true for heifer slaughter as well. A further 10 per cent to 12 per cent deletion in Saskatchewan's cow herd is expected this year. That will bring herd levels in that province back to 1970-71 levels, wiping out five years of gains toward a more diversified agricultural economy.
Consumers will see a return to the high prices of the early 1970's when the beef cycle hits its high point in 1978-79, as the government's so-called stabilization does nothing to stabilize the production of cattle at the farm level.
To pay $20 or so when some producers have had losses of up to $100 a head is no more than a political ploy. The cynicism of the federal plan is further demonstrated in the provision that producers enrolled in provincial programs will receive only half of the federal deficiency payment. While the government has consistently opposed toploading of federal stabilization plans, the minister can hardly claim that Manitoba, B.C., Ontario and Quebec are toploading his plan. They were instituted because the federal minister failed to bring in a plan of his own.
Returns to producers are higher in all the provincial plans than they will be under the federal scheme. Manitoba, which sends more than half its beef to central Canada, would have lost $4 million in federal payments in 1976 had the plan been in effect then. It makes no sense to penalize a province which brought in an imaginative and progressive plan to protect its beef industry in the absence of federal action. If medicare had been introduced on the same basis as this stabilization program, Saskatchewan would only be getting half the payments it now gets.

The time when federal-provincial relations are at their shakiest since Confederation is scarcely the time to add new injury to inaction. I can assure hon. members that representatives from all the provinces we talked to are very upset about this point. Manitoba taxpayers, for example, will continue to subsidize central Canadian consumers, as Alberta and Saskatchewan taxpayers did in 1976, to the tune of some $72 million.
The federal government cynically exploited the drop in beef prices as it moved the food index lower and gave the impression that the anti-inflation program was working. The beef index is just under three points in the consumer price index.
Meanwhile, back at the ranch, the minister's real heroes in the fight against inflation are taking a beating. Farmers all across the country have suffered income cuts, but beef producers are in especially desperate straits at this time. The 15,000 producers who have applied for payments under Saskatchewan's emergency plan had average taxable incomes of $1,600 in 1975. That is the kind of "powerful group" in society which has had to suffer the rough justice of restraint. The federal government must take the blame. It could have controlled imports, but it did not. It could have rationalized the country's beef marketing system, but it did not. Thousands of cow-calf operators are paying for this inaction now as they mortgage their family farms or go under in bankruptcy and, in a year or two, millions of Canadians will pay in higher prices at the supermarket. But between now and then is an election and maybe the Minister of Agriculture's $70 million sop will buy him some friends. I doubt it.
The second point I want to raise is the increase in community pasture rates by over 30 per cent in a year when beef prices are low and when we have an anti-inflation program. Farmers have just received notice that the PFRA community pasture rates administered by DREE will increase for cattle from nine cents per head per day to 12 cents per head per day, an increase of some 33 per cent. Breeding charges are going from $10 to $13 per day, an increase of 30 per cent. Delegations of farmers have protested to me the increase of over 30 per cent in a year when people are being told to tighten their belts, yet here is a federal government agency increasing the rate to farmers by over 30 per cent. That does not seem to be fair, especially when farmers are getting depressed prices for the beef they are forced to sell and the federal government says they must recover their costs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to call the attention of the House to a sentence the hon. member has just spoken and which I did not expect at all, as I am not following the text prepared by the department. The hon. member raised this point at a time when the problems of the Confederation are
January 31, 1977

being discussed at the provincial and federal levels. The hon. member said all this was the fault of the federal government and of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). On several occasions the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) asked the provinces to come to an agreement. He urged them to discuss the national program. He did not want a program unsatisfactory for most of the provinces. Therefore he asked them to come to an understanding first, after which it would be possible to develop a national program. So I think that the allegations of the hon. member are absolutely unfounded, as it is much too easy to cast all the blame for this on the minister. [English]
I am pleased to have this opportunity to respond to the incorrect allegations which the hon. member made about the federal cow-calf stabilization program in his question of January 27, 1977. This is an important program for the Canadian beef industry and it is essential that such misrepresentations are not given to Canadian farmers.
I wish, first, to emphasize that the program announced by the Minister of Agriculture on January 4, 1977, does not discriminate against farmers or provinces. From the farmer's point of view this program will ensure that producers in all provinces will receive stabilization benefits whether a program is, or is not, already in effect in his province. In this respect I am sure the hon. gentleman opposite will agree with me that the federal initiative in the cow-calf sector is a very positive step toward correcting discrimination and inequities which have existed among provinces in the past.
A producer who is enrolled in a provincial cow-calf program will receive the maximum net support possible under either the federal or the provincial program-whichever is greater. He will receive 50 per cent of the federal stabilization payment, with the remainder coming from the provincial government.
The federal program, which will cost an estimated $70 million, will relieve provincial treasuries of a significant portion of their commitment to producers. Producers will not only receive the full amounts guaranteed in their provincial plans but in those cases where the federal stabilization level is higher than that of the province, will receive larger payments than originally anticipated.
It would not have been fair to implement a federal program which had no benefits for producers already registered under provincial plans.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO PROTECT PUBLIC FROM EFFECTS OF EXCAVATION IN QUAKER CRESCENT AREA OF LOWER SACKVILLE
CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO PROTECT PUBLIC FROM EFFECTS OF EXCAVATION IN QUAKER CRESCENT AREA OF LOWER SACKVILLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, late last November and last month I mentioned the melancholy and sad events touching housing development in the commu-
Adjournment Debate
nity of lower Sackville in the constituency of Halifax-East Hants.
I pointed out that through the Nova Scotia Housing Commission people had been sold lots and promised land for a church, a 15 acre shopping centre, high rise and single family dwellings, a school, and amenities such as parkland. Subsequently the Nova Scotia Housing Commission entered into a deal. The 15 acre shopping centre swallowed up all the land and removed the school and apartment buildings and the place for other single homes, as well as the parkland. I suggest that was a gross breach of promise to the people who had bought in all good faith and depended on the plans presented by the housing commission. I thought that was dishonest. I also said that the company entering into this deal had done so without taking part in any tendering proceedings. The company was actually formed after the original deal was made. Two friends of the minister of housing for Nova Scotia formed the company, to acquire the land. I said this was corrupt.
The Nova Scotia Housing Commission was good enough to let me see its files. I found, that the very first document which ought to have been on record is missing. That has not caused me to withdraw or soften the complaints I made.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation had poured millions of dollars into that development through grants that it made to the Nova Scotia Housing Commission, to enable land to be assembled in the first place, and with mortgages made available to homeowners when they began to build. A great deal of federal money is therefore at stake, which is why I have been raising this question in the House of Commons.
When the concept of the shopping centre expanded from one involving 15 acres to one involving 21 acres, bulldozers moved in; along the rear lines of the lots on two streets, Quaker Crescent and Polara Drive, a wall has been created, some of it is up to 30 feet high. The wall is holding back a sort of clay soil. The contractor has attempted to shore up this wall. Indeed, I gather that he plans to put a wire fence along the top of it. But the people who bought on Quaker Crescent and Polara Drive expected to be able to look down a gentle slope, through birch trees, walkways and other single family dwellings looking onto a lake. It was to be a pleasant neighbourhood prospect. Instead, they will face one of the largest Dominion stores in eastern Canada. It will be smack up against their properties, as will the other buildings of the shopping centre nearby.
The Nova Scota Housing Comission said, in its defence, that it was only making proposals when it presented plans to the homeowners. The plan, signed by the Nova Scotia Housing Commission was, they say, only a proposal. This brought forth what I consider the best line in the public dialogue which has been created since I raised this issue in mid-November, when Councillor Francene Cosman of Bedford, which is nearby, said that if that was the proposal well, she, herself had once been proposed to and she took that proposal seriously.
2576

Adjournment Debate
I said that great hurt has been done to property values by reason of this desecration of what was originally a fine neighbourhood concept. This must also hurt the investment in that area of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I can suggest three remedies; two, not being germane to this House, I shall mention only briefly. In order to protect the public there must be some change in the law in the province of Nova Scotia. That province cannot depend on a minister of housing whose association with the developers makes Damon and Pythias seem like mortal enemies. Second, provincial and municipal laws must be changed so that the public is protected.
We come into the picture in relation to the third point and I hope the parliamentary secretary will raise this question with CMHC. I do not disagree with the role CMHC has played in this matter. As a matter of fact, any opinion I have had from the minister or the parliamentary secretary has been sympathetic to the homeowners because of the nature of the promises made to them. But I think that if federal moneys go through CMHC to provincial housing corporations or commissions we should insist that very strong agreements are made so that we may know exactly what that federal money would be used for. It simply cannot be left to be administered by a provincial housing minister as though he were running an old pals' act.
All this has led to a lot of frustration among the people concerned. They feel alienated. They say, "The developer is too big for us to deal with." They say the minister of housing is too important for them to be able to deal with. Some of that frustration has boiled over on myself. I know the developer has attacked me in a long front page letter published in the Halifax Mail-Star. My reply has not yet seen the light of day
in that same newspaper, so the newspaper will obviously not be very helpful in this fight. Nonetheless, by boiling over here, and perhaps in other places, we may yet civilize developers and get a better deal for those who put their life savings into housing. At least that will be my endeavour.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO PROTECT PUBLIC FROM EFFECTS OF EXCAVATION IN QUAKER CRESCENT AREA OF LOWER SACKVILLE

Mr. Speaker, in my response in the House on November 30 on the subject the hon. member has raised, I replied in some detail setting out the position of CMHC with respect to this project. I am sure he does not want me to repeat my words. I might add that after making my response I spoke to the hon. member and suggested that the matter of the residents' rights in this controversy might be taken up with the ombudsman in Nova Scotia. It goes without saying that if the Nova Scotia Housing Commission has disregarded any legal obligation to the residents, they should consider seeking an injunction, or other appropriate legal action. Not being a lawyer, I hesitate to go any further in giving advice to the hon. member.
I take note of his remarks concerning the need for a strengthening of the agreements with regard to development projects and I will bring the hon. member's comments to the attention of my minister. I should like to tell the hon. member's comments to the attention of my minister. I should like to tell the hon. member that CMHC is not in the business of running municipal councils and that zoning is not our business, but I repeat that if there are legal problems here which demand further action, the proper course, I suspect, would be for him to take the matter up with the people concerned and advise them as to the possibility of going to the ombudsman.
